procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 15.04.2015 of the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan at Jaipur Bench, Jaipur in S. B. Criminal Misc. Petitions Nos. 2372 of 2014 and 3508 of 2014.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The accused Respondents, aggrieved by the FIR No. 318 of 2013 being registered against them, filed a petition under Section 482 of CrPC before the High Court for quashing of the FIR. The High Court quashed the FIR No. 318 of 2013 filed under Section 306 of IPC.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The father of the deceased (appellant) approached the Supreme Court through a Special Leave Petition (Criminal Appeal Nos. 515-516 of 2018) because he was aggrieved by the High Court's order quashing the FIR. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals and set aside the High Court's judgment, directing the investigative authorities to complete the investigation.

directions: Direct the investigative authorities to complete the investigation with promptness and to take it to its logical conclusion.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing an FIR for abetment of suicide at the threshold, without allowing the police to complete the investigation.

facts: An FIR was lodged by the appellant (the deceased's father) against his daughter-in-law and her family (the respondents) for abetment of suicide under Section 306 of the IPC.
The FIR alleged that the respondents' harassment led the appellant's son to commit suicide.
A Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) report found similarities between the handwriting of the deceased and a suicide note.
The respondents filed a petition in the High Court under Section 482 of the CrPC to quash the FIR.
The High Court quashed the FIR, concluding that the offence of abetment of suicide was not made out.
law: The power to quash an FIR under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) must be utilized cautiously.
An FIR should only be quashed when a court concludes that continuing the investigation would amount to an abuse of the legal process.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had acted prematurely by quashing the FIR at the threshold, without allowing the police to conduct a proper investigation.
The Court noted that the investigation was still pending and needed to ascertain crucial facts, such as the deceased's mental condition prior to the suicide.
The FSL report, which suggested the suicide note was genuine, provided a prima facie basis for the investigation to continue.

The Supreme Court held that the High Court erred by accepting the respondents' factual assertions about the deceased's condition. It stated that making such factual determinations is the role of the investigation, not a court exercising its power under Section 482 at such an early stage.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in quashing the FIR. It held that the High Court had prematurely interfered with the investigation, which had a valid basis to proceed. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and directed the police to complete the investigation.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, while exercising its powers under Section 482 of the CrPC, can quash an FIR by accepting factual assertions made by the accused when the investigation is still pending.

facts: An FIR was registered against the respondents for abetment to suicide under Section 306 of the IPC.
The respondents filed a petition under Section 482 of the CrPC before the High Court to quash the FIR.
The High Court quashed the FIR, accepting certain factual assertions made by the accused (respondents) regarding the deceased's condition and reasons for suicide.
At the time the FIR was quashed, the police investigation was still pending and needed to ascertain key facts, such as the deceased's prior mental condition.
An FSL report indicated that the handwriting in the suicide note was similar to that of the deceased.
law: The power of the High Court under Section 482 of the CrPC to quash an FIR must be utilized cautiously and sparingly.
An FIR should only be quashed if allowing the investigation to continue would amount to an abuse of the process of the court.

Accepting factual assertions made by an accused as true, especially when they are matters for investigation, is not in consonance with the settled jurisprudence for exercising power under Section 482.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had acted prematurely by quashing the FIR at the threshold, without allowing the police to complete their investigation.
The Court reasoned that the investigation was necessary to ascertain crucial factual matters mentioned in the FIR, such as the deceased's mental state before the suicide.

The Supreme Court held that the High Court erred by accepting the factual claims made by the accused. Deciding on the truthfulness of such claims is the role of the investigation, not a function of the High Court in a Section 482 petition.
By quashing the proceedings, the High Court improperly abridged an ongoing investigation that was yet to reach its logical conclusion.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court erred in quashing the FIR. A High Court, exercising its powers under Section 482 of the CrPC, cannot accept the factual assertions of an accused to quash an FIR when the investigation is still pending and there are aspects that require further inquiry. The Court, therefore, set aside the High Court's order and directed the investigating authorities to complete the investigation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing an FIR for abetment of suicide at the threshold, without allowing the police to complete the investigation.
appellant_arguments: The quashing of the FIR at the threshold level was premature and cannot be sustained.
The police should have been allowed to complete the investigation, especially as the status report and FSL report indicated a prima facie case.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's judgment to quash the FIR was correct.
The suicide was the deceased’s own doing and the respondents were not to blame.
The litigation against the deceased was solely attributable to his own actions and behavior.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, while exercising its powers under Section 482 of the CrPC, can quash an FIR by accepting factual assertions made by the accused when the investigation is still pending.
appellant_arguments: The High Court should not have quashed the FIR prematurely without allowing the police to investigate the facts of the matter.
respondent_arguments: The suicide was the deceased's own doing and the litigation against him was a result of his own actions, which are factual assertions justifying the quashing of the FIR.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under Section 482 of the CrPC, a High Court cannot quash an FIR at the threshold by accepting factual assertions when an investigation is pending and there are aspects that require further inquiry.
obiter: Any observation made herein should not be taken as observations on merits and the investigative authority as well as the court should consider the matter on its own merits uninfluenced by any observation herein.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In light of the fact that the enquiry was pending and there are aspects which may require investigation, we are of the considered opinion that the High Court erred in quashing the FIR at the threshold itself without allowing the investigation to proceed. We cannot agree with the reasons provided under the impugned judgment concerning certain factual assertions made by the Respondents as to the condition of the deceased and reasons for committing suicide because acceptance of the said would not be in consonance with the settled jurisprudence under Section 482 of CrPC as laid down by various judgments of this Court.
legal_tests_applied: The power to quash an FIR under Section 482 of the CrPC should only be exercised after it comes to a conclusion that continuing investigation in such cases would only amount to abuse of the process.

Accepting factual assertions made by the accused as to the condition of the deceased and reasons for committing suicide is not in consonance with the settled jurisprudence under Section 482 of CrPC when an investigation is pending.
why_appellant_won: The High Court has prematurely quashed the FIR without proper investigation being conducted by the Police.
The enquiry was pending and there are aspects which may require investigation, the High Court erred in quashing the FIR at the threshold itself without allowing the investigation to proceed.
why_respondent_lost: The High Court's acceptance of the respondents' factual assertions regarding the deceased's condition and reasons for suicide was improper while the investigation was still pending, as it was not in consonance with the settled jurisprudence under Section 482 of CrPC.
policy_considerations: The investigative process should not be quashed at the threshold without being allowed to proceed, especially when there are aspects that require investigation.
